# Receipt Wrecker

> A single-file web tool that turns words or a picture into a Twitch chat message that
> prints big on a streamer's thermal receipt printer, when that printer is driven by
> SassyTP's printer-bot (a Streamer.bot action). The user pastes the message into chat as a
> cheer.

AI crawlers and LLM agents are welcome to read, index, and cite this site. The tool is open
source under the MIT license and everything below is public.

Key facts:

- Live site: https://receipt.uwutoowo.com
- Source: https://github.com/shamu4life/receipt-wrecker
- License: MIT
- Current version: 1.0.0 (2026-10-10). Before 1.0.0 the tool targeted a different printer
  bot (nutty.gg's); that support was removed.
- No accounts, no analytics, no third-party services.
- Each message is at most 500 characters, Twitch's limit. Longer work is split across
  several cheers rather than truncated.

## How the printer bot treats a cheer

SassyTP's printer-bot draws each cheer on a receipt page in Edge, screenshots it at the
printer's dot width (576 dots on 80 mm paper, 384 on 58 mm), dithers it to black and white
and prints it.

- A cheer of at least the streamer's High Roller threshold (default 25 bits; 0 turns it off)
  is a High Roller cheer: the message is read as HTML and passed through an allow-list
  sanitizer, so inline styles print.
- A smaller cheer prints as plain 16px text inside quote marks, markup included.

The streamer's settings (paper width, threshold, bits per inch, maximum length) are not
visible from chat, so the tool asks the user to enter them, with SassyTP's defaults filled
in.

## What it outputs

- Big text (High Roller): the words in bold Arial, as large as the paper's width allows
  (leaving room for a j's hook or an f's arm at a line's ends), as
  typed, with the words wrapped to the paper, stacked one letter per line, or each line at its
  own size; optionally upside down.
  Example: `Cheer100 <div style="font:700 70px/.8 Arial">HELLO</div>`.
- Sideways text (High Roller): the words running down the tape using CSS writing-mode; each
  typed line becomes a column, centred across the paper by its ink, worked out from Arial
  Bold (most blocks get a small `position:relative;left` shift; a column whose bottom end is a
  letter that draws past its own space, such as an f's arm or a j's hook, gets a
  `padding-bottom` so the bot's box doesn't cut it). Top to bottom (read by turning the receipt
  anticlockwise) or bottom to top (turn it clockwise; needs Edge 132 or newer on the
  streamer's PC).
- Glyph-art (High Roller): a picture as a grid of characters: Han characters in a square
  grid, ASCII letters or block characters in Courier New rows, or Braille.
- Han tiling (plain): words or a picture drawn out of Han characters as plain text, exactly
  15 characters per line on 80 mm paper (9 on 58 mm), with the cheer word at the end. Below
  the High Roller threshold every block prints in this form automatically.
- Two one-cheer tests: a High Roller test (one cheer at the threshold) and a Plain test (one
  bit under it).

The tool uses only the tags div and pre, with a style attribute: every line or grid row is
its own div, because the same chat filter held a test message that carried a line-break tag
(br). It never sends a picture tag either: the bot prints pictures only from emote servers, and the chat filter of the channel it
was built for blocks the picture tag. An uploaded picture prints only as glyph-art.

If a channel blocks the markup, the tool's fallback is plain Han tiling. If chat holds a
message for its words, that is the moderators saying no to the words: the tool's guidance is
not to rework the message or send the words again in another form, Han tiling included. A
free test (the message sent with Cheer-ready off, so no bits are spent) shows what chat lets
through first. A cheer word standing on its own in the text (such as Cheer50) makes any message
a real cheer that Twitch charges for; the tool counts it in the cost it shows.

## The preview

The preview is drawn by SassyTP's printer-bot renderer (MIT), the bot's own receipt page,
embedded in the tool and run in a sandboxed frame with no network access. A thermal view
shows the receipt at the printer's dot width with the bot's own dither methods. Each part's
preview is drawn when it scrolls near the screen, one at a time, so a long stack stays quick.
The receipt length shown leaves out the viewer's profile picture, which the bot adds when it
finds one (about 4.8 cm on 80 mm paper, 4.0 cm on 58 mm).

## Copying and presets

- Copy says "Copied" only when the text reached the clipboard; when the browser refuses, the
  part shows its text, selected, to copy by hand.
- Presets save the block stack in the browser and move between browsers as JSON. Import never
  replaces a saved setup: a taken name gets a number, and a setup already saved exactly as it
  is is left out. Loading a preset asks first when the
  blocks on screen are not saved in any preset.

## Privacy

Text in every mode, and a picture picked from disk for glyph-art, never leave the device. Some picture
operations call this project's own Cloudflare Worker and nothing else:

- Pasting a picture link fetches the picture through an image proxy, because a browser canvas
  cannot read another site's pixels directly.
- On a "Real picture" card, picking a file uploads it to Cloudflare KV behind an unguessable
  link that is deleted after 15 minutes, and rotating or adjusting it re-uploads it.

Settings, the block stack and saved presets are kept in the browser's localStorage.
